subject: Computer Science
summary: Covers display hardware (CRT, raster/random scan, flat panels, colour models), line and circle algorithms (DDA, Bresenham, midpoint), 2D/3D transformations and projections, clipping (Cohen-Sutherland, Liang-Barsky, Sutherland-Hodgman), curves, hidden-surface removal and shading, and multimedia digitisation, compression and file formats. Exams mix definition questions (CRT parts, resolution, emissive displays, formats) with short numericals on algorithms, transformations and colour conversion.

sections.heading: Display devices: CRT, raster and random scan
sections.body:
**CRT** (Cathode Ray Tube) parts, in order along the beam:
- **Heating filament** heats the **cathode**, which emits electrons (together, the electron gun).
- **Control grid** - a negatively charged cylinder that regulates the number of electrons, i.e. the **intensity (brightness)** of the beam.
- **Focusing anode / system** - converges the beam to a small spot.
- **Accelerating anode** - accelerates electrons towards the screen.
- **Deflection plates or coils** (horizontal and vertical) - steer the beam.
- **Phosphor-coated screen** - glows where the beam strikes.

Key terms: **persistence** - time for emitted light to decay to one-tenth of its original intensity (low persistence needs a higher refresh rate); **refresh rate** - screen redraws per second (Hz); **resolution** - the maximum number of points that can be displayed **without overlap**; **aspect ratio** - ratio of horizontal to vertical points (or width : height); **pixel** (picture element) - smallest addressable screen point.

**Raster scan** - beam sweeps the screen row by row (scan lines) from top to bottom; picture stored as intensity values in the **frame buffer** (refresh buffer); horizontal retrace at the end of each line, vertical retrace at the end of each frame; interlacing draws odd lines then even lines. Good for realistic shaded scenes; lines may show jaggies (aliasing).
**Random scan (vector / calligraphic)** - beam draws only the lines of the picture, stored as a **display file** (display list); smooth lines, but cannot show realistic shaded areas.

Colour CRTs: **beam penetration** (red and green phosphor layers, few colours, used with random scan) and **shadow mask** (RGB phosphor triads with three guns, used with raster systems).

rows: Draws whole screen line by line
Refresh time depends on number of lines

sections.heading: Flat panels, frame buffer and input devices
sections.body:
**Flat-panel displays**:
- **Emissive** (convert electrical energy into light): **plasma panels**, **LED** displays, **thin-film electroluminescent** displays.
- **Non-emissive** (use optical effects to modulate external/back light): **LCD** (liquid crystal display, uses polarised light through liquid crystal).

**Frame buffer size** = horizontal resolution × vertical resolution × bits per pixel (÷ 8 for bytes). With *n* bits per pixel, 2ⁿ colours/intensities are possible. A **colour look-up table** lets a small pixel value index a larger palette.

**Input devices**: keyboard, mouse, trackball, **spaceball** (6 degrees of freedom), **joystick**, **data glove**, **digitizer / graphics tablet**, **light pen** (detects light from the screen to pick positions), touch panel, image scanner, voice systems. Sensors in phones: **gyroscope** detects orientation and angular velocity, **accelerometer** detects linear acceleration, **magnetometer** detects the magnetic field (compass), **proximity sensor** detects nearby objects.

**Colour models**: **RGB** - additive (monitors); **CMY** - subtractive (printers), with **(C, M, Y) = (1, 1, 1) − (R, G, B)**; **CMYK** adds black; **HSV/HSB** (hue, saturation, value) and **HLS** - intuitive for users; **YIQ** - NTSC television.

sections.heading: Line drawing: DDA and Bresenham
sections.body:
Scan conversion = choosing the pixels that best approximate a primitive.

**DDA (Digital Differential Analyzer)**: steps = max(|Δx|, |Δy|); x_inc = Δx ÷ steps, y_inc = Δy ÷ steps; starting at (x₁, y₁) repeatedly add the increments and **round** each coordinate. Simple, but uses floating-point additions and rounding, so it is slower and round-off error can accumulate on long lines.

**Bresenham's line algorithm** (for slope 0 ≤ m ≤ 1, x₁ < x₂) uses **only integer addition/subtraction and multiplication by 2**:
- Plot (x₁, y₁); decision parameter **p₀ = 2Δy − Δx**.
- At each step x increases by 1. If **pₖ < 0**: next point (xₖ+1, yₖ) and **pₖ₊₁ = pₖ + 2Δy**. Otherwise: next point (xₖ+1, yₖ+1) and **pₖ₊₁ = pₖ + 2Δy − 2Δx**.
- Repeat Δx times.
For |m| > 1 swap the roles of x and y; other octants follow by symmetry.

The **midpoint line algorithm** gives the same pixels as Bresenham, derived by testing the midpoint between candidate pixels.

sections.heading: Circle drawing: midpoint algorithm and symmetry
sections.body:
A circle is **8-way symmetric**: computing points in one octant (from x = 0 to x = y) gives the rest as (±x, ±y) and (±y, ±x), shifted by the centre (x_c, y_c).

**Midpoint circle algorithm** (centre at origin, radius r, start (0, r)):
- **p₀ = 1 − r** (from 5/4 − r rounded for integer r).
- At each step x increases by 1. If **pₖ < 0**: y unchanged, **pₖ₊₁ = pₖ + 2xₖ₊₁ + 1**. Otherwise: y decreases by 1, **pₖ₊₁ = pₖ + 2xₖ₊₁ + 1 − 2yₖ₊₁**.
- Stop when x ≥ y.
Finally add (x_c, y_c) to every point. **Bresenham's circle algorithm** is an equivalent integer method with initial decision parameter d = 3 − 2r.

**Ellipse** (midpoint ellipse) uses 4-way symmetry and two regions split where the slope equals −1.

**Polygon filling**: scan-line fill (intersections of each scan line with edges, filled in pairs), **boundary fill** (fill until boundary colour is reached) and **flood fill** (replace an interior colour), each using 4-connected or 8-connected neighbours.

sections.heading: 2D transformations and homogeneous coordinates
sections.body:
Using **homogeneous coordinates** (x, y, 1), every 2D transformation is a 3×3 matrix, so a sequence of transformations can be combined (concatenated) into one matrix. With column vectors, P′ = M · P.

- **Translation**: x′ = x + tₓ, y′ = y + t_y.
- **Scaling** about the origin: x′ = sₓ·x, y′ = s_y·y (sₓ = s_y gives uniform scaling; values < 1 shrink and move the object towards the origin).
- **Rotation** by θ anticlockwise about the origin: x′ = x cos θ − y sin θ, y′ = x sin θ + y cos θ. Matrix [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]; for clockwise rotation replace θ by −θ.
- **Reflection**: about x-axis (x, −y); about y-axis (−x, y); about origin (−x, −y); about y = x → (y, x); about y = −x → (−y, −x).
- **Shear**: x-shear x′ = x + shₓ·y; y-shear y′ = y + sh_y·x.

**Composite transformations**: rotation or scaling about a fixed/pivot point (x_r, y_r) = **T(x_r, y_r) · R(θ) · T(−x_r, −y_r)** (translate to origin, transform, translate back). Successive translations add, successive rotations add angles, successive scalings multiply. Matrix multiplication is generally **not commutative**, so order matters.

**2D viewing pipeline**: construct the world-coordinate scene using modelling transformations → convert world coordinates to viewing coordinates → map viewing coordinates to normalised viewport coordinates (window-to-viewport mapping) → map the normalised viewport to device coordinates. A **window** is the world area selected for display; a **viewport** is the screen area where it is shown.

sections.heading: 3D transformations and projections
sections.body:
3D transformations use 4×4 homogeneous matrices. Rotation is about an axis: about the **z-axis** x′ = x cos θ − y sin θ, y′ = x sin θ + y cos θ, z′ = z (similarly for x and y axes).

**Projection** maps 3D to a 2D view plane:
- **Parallel projection** - projectors are parallel; preserves relative proportions, not realistic. **Orthographic** (projectors perpendicular to the view plane: front, top, side views; **axonometric** such as **isometric**, where all three axes are equally foreshortened) and **oblique** (projectors at an angle: **cavalier** - receding lines full length; **cabinet** - receding lines half length).
- **Perspective projection** - projectors converge at the **centre of projection**; distant objects look smaller (foreshortening), realistic. Parallel lines not parallel to the view plane meet at **vanishing points**: one-, two- or three-point perspective.

In engineering drawing, a plane surface perpendicular to the plane of projection appears as a **straight line** (its edge view) on that plane.

sections.heading: Clipping: point, line and polygon
sections.body:
**Clipping** identifies the parts of a picture inside or outside a specified region (the clip window); the visible portion is kept and the invisible portion discarded. It can be applied in world coordinates (before mapping) or to the viewport/device coordinates.

**Point clipping**: keep (x, y) if xmin ≤ x ≤ xmax and ymin ≤ y ≤ ymax.

**Cohen-Sutherland line clipping** assigns each endpoint a 4-bit **region code** (outcode), bits written as **TBRL** (bit 4 Top, bit 3 Bottom, bit 2 Right, bit 1 Left):
- Top = 1 if y > ymax; Bottom = 1 if y < ymin; Right = 1 if x > xmax; Left = 1 if x < xmin.
- Both codes 0000 → **trivially accept**.
- Logical **AND** of the two codes ≠ 0000 → both endpoints share an outside region → **trivially reject**.
- Otherwise pick an outside endpoint, intersect with the window edge given by a set bit (slope m = Δy ÷ Δx): vertical edge x = x_e gives y = y₁ + m(x_e − x₁); horizontal edge y = y_e gives x = x₁ + (y_e − y₁) ÷ m. Replace the endpoint, recompute its code and repeat.

**Liang-Barsky** uses the parametric form x = x₁ + uΔx, y = y₁ + uΔy (0 ≤ u ≤ 1) with pₖ, qₖ values; it needs fewer intersection calculations and is usually more efficient. **Cyrus-Beck** works for any convex window. **Midpoint subdivision** repeatedly halves the line.

**Polygon clipping**: **Sutherland-Hodgman** clips the polygon against each window edge in turn (correct for convex clip windows; a concave polygon can produce extraneous edges); **Weiler-Atherton** handles concave polygons. **Text clipping**: all-or-none string, all-or-none character, or clip individual character components.

sections.heading: Curves, surfaces and solid modelling
sections.body:
**Bezier curve**: with n + 1 control points the curve is a polynomial of **degree n** (Bernstein blending functions). It **passes through the first and last control points**, is tangent there to the first and last control-polygon edges, and lies inside the **convex hull** of the control points. Control is **global**: moving one point changes the whole curve. Cubic Bezier uses 4 control points.

**B-spline curve**: degree is independent of the number of control points, gives **local control** (moving a point affects only nearby segments), lies in the convex hull, and in general does not pass through the end control points (unless clamped/open-uniform).

**Hermite curve**: defined by two endpoints and the tangent vectors at them. **Continuity**: C⁰ (curves meet), C¹ (equal first derivative), C² (equal second derivative); geometric G⁰, G¹.

**Surface interpolation methods** (estimating unknown values from known sample points, as in GIS/terrain modelling): Inverse Distance Weighted (IDW: nearer points have more weight), Kriging (statistical), Natural Neighbor, Spline (smooth surface through points) and Topo to Raster.

**Surfaces and solids**: polygon meshes, quadric surfaces (sphere, ellipsoid), Bezier and B-spline surfaces, sweep representations, **CSG** (Constructive Solid Geometry: union, intersection, difference of primitives), **B-rep** (boundary representation), octrees. A solid-modelling representation must be **complete, valid and unambiguous**.

sections.heading: Hidden surfaces, shading and animation
sections.body:
**Visible-surface (hidden-surface) detection** methods:
- **Object-space** methods compare objects or their parts: **back-face detection** (discard polygons whose normal points away from the viewer).
- **Image-space** methods decide visibility pixel by pixel: **Z-buffer (depth buffer)**, A-buffer, scan-line, **area subdivision (Warnock)**, ray casting.
- **Depth-sort (painter's) algorithm** works in both spaces: sort surfaces by depth and paint the farthest first.

**Z-buffer algorithm**: uses a **depth buffer** (depth per pixel) and the **frame/refresh buffer** (colour per pixel). Initialise every depth to the farthest value and every colour to the background; for each polygon and each pixel it covers, compute the depth z; if z is nearer than the stored depth, store z and the polygon's colour. No sorting needed and any number of polygons can be processed one at a time, but it needs memory for a full depth buffer and deals with one visible surface per pixel (no transparency in the basic form).

**Illumination and shading**: ambient light; **diffuse reflection** (Lambert's cosine law: intensity ∝ cos θ between light direction and surface normal); **specular reflection** (Phong model, highlights). **Flat (constant) shading** - one intensity per polygon; **Gouraud shading** - interpolate **intensities** across the polygon (smooth, may miss highlights, Mach bands); **Phong shading** - interpolate **normal vectors** (better highlights, more computation).

**Animation**: key frames with **in-betweening (tweening)** to create intermediate frames; **morphing** transforms one shape into another; frame-by-frame animation; motion capture.

sections.heading: Multimedia: digitisation and compression
sections.body:
**Multimedia** combines text, images/graphics, audio, video and animation, usually with interactivity; **hypermedia** adds links between them.

**Digitisation** of analog media uses two steps: **sampling** (measuring the signal at regular time intervals; sampling rate in Hz) and **quantisation** (rounding each sample to one of 2ⁿ levels, n = bits per sample). **Nyquist theorem**: sample at least **twice the highest frequency** to reconstruct the signal (audio CD: 44.1 kHz, 16-bit, stereo).

**Raster (bitmap)** images store pixels and blur when enlarged; **vector** images store shapes as equations and scale without loss (SVG).

**Data compression** reduces the size of multimedia files:
- **Lossless** - original recovered exactly: run-length encoding (RLE), Huffman coding, LZW, arithmetic coding (PNG, GIF, ZIP, FLAC).
- **Lossy** - discards less noticeable information for much higher ratios: JPEG (DCT + quantisation), MP3 (psychoacoustic model), MPEG video (I, P and B frames using inter-frame prediction).
- Compression ratio = original size ÷ compressed size.

**Streaming protocols**: **RTP** (Real-time Transport Protocol) is the basic protocol for transmitting real-time audio/video, usually over UDP; **RTCP** carries control and quality feedback; **RTSP** (Real Time Streaming Protocol) gives play/pause/seek control.

formulas.name: DDA increments
formulas.formula: steps = max(|Δx|, |Δy|);  x_inc = Δx ÷ steps;  y_inc = Δy ÷ steps

formulas.name: Bresenham line (0 ≤ m ≤ 1)
formulas.formula: p₀ = 2Δy − Δx; p < 0 → p += 2Δy; else y++ and p += 2Δy − 2Δx
formulas.note: x increases by 1 every step; Δx steps in total.

formulas.name: Midpoint circle
formulas.formula: p₀ = 1 − r; p < 0 → p += 2x + 1; else y−− and p += 2x + 1 − 2y
formulas.note: x and y are the new values; stop when x ≥ y.

formulas.name: Rotation about origin
formulas.formula: x′ = x cosθ − y sinθ;  y′ = x sinθ + y cosθ

formulas.name: Fixed-point scaling
formulas.formula: x′ = x_f + sₓ(x − x_f);  y′ = y_f + s_y(y − y_f)

formulas.name: Window to viewport
formulas.note: Similarly for y; the ratio is the scaling factor sₓ.

formulas.name: Frame buffer size
formulas.formula: bits = width × height × bits per pixel; colours = 2^(bits per pixel)

formulas.name: Uncompressed audio size
formulas.formula: bytes = sampling rate × (bits per sample ÷ 8) × channels × seconds

workedExamples.problem: Practice: Scan-convert the line from (2, 3) to (8, 7) using (a) DDA and (b) Bresenham.
Practice: Use the midpoint circle algorithm for r = 8, centre (0, 0), to find the first-octant pixels.
workedExamples.solution:
Start (0, 8), p₀ = 1 − 8 = −7.
- p = −7 < 0 → (1, 8); new p = −7 + 2(1) + 1 = −4
- p = −4 < 0 → (2, 8); p = −4 + 2(2) + 1 = 1
- p = 1 ≥ 0 → (3, 7); p = 1 + 2(3) + 1 − 2(7) = −6
- p = −6 < 0 → (4, 7); p = −6 + 2(4) + 1 = 3
- p = 3 ≥ 0 → (5, 6); p = 3 + 2(5) + 1 − 2(6) = 2
- p = 2 ≥ 0 → next would be (6, 5), where x > y, so the octant ends.
First-octant pixels: (0,8) (1,8) (2,8) (3,7) (4,7) (5,6). The other seven octants follow by symmetry; for centre (x_c, y_c) add it to every point.

workedExamples.problem: Practice: Window xmin = 10, xmax = 50, ymin = 10, ymax = 40. Clip the line P₁(5, 20) to P₂(60, 45) with Cohen-Sutherland.
workedExamples.solution:
Codes (TBRL): P₁: x < 10 → **0001**. P₂: y > 40 (Top) and x > 50 (Right) → **1010**.
AND = 0000 (not trivially rejected); codes not both 0000 (not trivially accepted) → clip.
Slope m = (45 − 20) ÷ (60 − 5) = 25/55 = 5/11.
- P₁ against left edge x = 10: y = 20 + (5/11)(10 − 5) = 20 + 2.27 = 22.27 → (10, 22.27), code 0000.
- P₂ against top edge y = 40: x = 5 + (40 − 20) ÷ (5/11) = 5 + 44 = 49 → (49, 40), code 0000.
(If the right edge is processed first: y = 20 + (5/11)(45) = 40.45, code 1000, then the top edge gives (49, 40) again.)
Visible segment: **(10, 22.27) to (49, 40)**.

workedExamples.problem: Practice: Rotate the point (5, 3) by 90° anticlockwise about the pivot (2, 1). Also scale the point (2, 3) by sₓ = 2, s_y = 3 about the fixed point (1, 1).
Practice: Map the world point (60, 70) from window (10, 20)-(110, 120) to viewport (100, 100)-(300, 200).

pitfalls: Control grid controls beam intensity; the focusing anode focuses; the accelerating anode accelerates.
Resolution = maximum points displayable without overlap; persistence = decay time of phosphor glow.
LCD is non-emissive; plasma, LED and thin-film electroluminescent displays are emissive.
DDA uses floating point and rounding; Bresenham uses only integer operations.
Bresenham: p < 0 keeps y; p ≥ 0 increments y. Do not swap the two update formulas.
Cohen-Sutherland: trivial reject uses logical AND ≠ 0, not OR; OR = 0 means trivial accept.
Rotation and translation do not commute: T·R ≠ R·T in general.
Bezier curves pass through only the first and last control points and have global control; B-splines give local control.
Z-buffer is an image-space method; back-face detection is object-space; painter's algorithm uses both.
Gouraud interpolates intensities; Phong interpolates normals.
MP3 is MPEG Audio Layer III (.mp3), not MPEG-3; MP4 is a container from MPEG-4.
GIF supports only 256 colours; JPEG is lossy; PNG and GIF are lossless.
quickRevision: Pixel = picture element; frame buffer stores pixel intensities.
Raster scan: frame buffer, scan lines; random scan: display file, smooth lines.
Aspect ratio = width : height (or horizontal : vertical points).
Colours with n bits per pixel = 2ⁿ.
CMY = 1 − RGB; RGB is additive, CMY subtractive.
Bresenham p₀ = 2Δy − Δx; midpoint circle p₀ = 1 − r.
Rotation about a pivot: translate to origin, rotate, translate back.
Region code bits: Top, Bottom, Right, Left; inside = 0000.
Sutherland-Hodgman: polygon clipping edge by edge; Weiler-Atherton: concave polygons.
Z-buffer needs a depth buffer plus a frame buffer.
Digitisation = sampling + quantisation; Nyquist rate = 2 × highest frequency.
RTP = Real-time Transport Protocol for audio/video delivery.
